column3: [tense] Your little brother is three meters from a garbage truck. And he hasn't seen it.
To you, the truck is barely moving. You have sixteen whole minutes to save him.
[quickly] Easy, right? Just grab him and run.
[nervous] Except if you grab him at your speed… you'll hit him harder than the truck would.
[whispers] The fastest person who has ever lived. And the only way to save him… is slowly.
We'll come back to this.
[calm] It starts on a Monday. You hit snooze three times. You always do. You're the kid who's late for everything.
[calling from downstairs] You're going to be late!
[curious] So what if, every day, you got ten times faster? Day two, ten times. Day three, a hundred. Day ten… [short pause] a billion.
Here's how it works. Every time you wake up, everything about you is ten times faster. Your legs, your hands, your brain, your heart. The world stays exactly the same.
But that's tomorrow. [short pause] Remember this Monday. It's the last normal day you'll ever have.
Breakfast. Your mom has written the same thing on the fridge for two weeks. Tuesday. Nine o'clock. Candles.
Your little brother was born at exactly nine in the morning. So every year, the candles go out at exactly nine. It's the rule.
Don't be late for my candles.
You promise. [short pause] Remember that promise.
You know why you're always late? [short pause] Because you're never early.
That's not a joke, Dad. That's just a sentence.
You run for the bus. The bus wins. It always wins.
[grinning] Race you tomorrow?
He asks every day. You lose every day.
[mocking] Nice run, Snail.
Snail. Your nickname since fifth grade.
If you fold a thousand paper cranes, you get one wish.
[warmly] He's folded four. And you still don't have a present for him.
Monday dinner. Grandpa tells his fishing story. It takes forty minutes. It always does.
[whispers] At eleven, you fall asleep. For the last time as a normal kid.
Day two. You wake up at six twenty. Before your alarm. That has never happened. Ever.
You knock over your water glass. And you have time to catch it… look at it… and scoop the water back in.
This part is real. A normal person needs about a quarter of a second to react. That's why you can't catch a falling glass. Today, ten times faster, you need a fortieth.
At first, you think the house is broken. The clock on the wall ticks… and ticks… way too slowly. The toaster takes twenty minutes.
Everyone's still asleep. And you are SO hungry. Moving ten times faster doesn't cost ten times the energy. It costs a hundred.
So you go for a run. Just a jog. [short pause] Two hundred and fifty kilometers an hour. About as fast as a Formula One car.
[laughs] You overtake a delivery van. On foot. The driver will be telling this story for the rest of his life.
And you pass the bus. [short pause] For the first time in your life, you win.
Then you remember. [short pause] The present.
For your family, it's one more hour of sleep. For you, it's ten. So you fold. A thousand paper cranes.
Then it starts to rain. And the raindrops are… floating. You hold out your hand, and a drop lands in it. Slowly. Like it's asking permission.
True story: a raindrop falls at about nine meters per second. At ten times your speed, it falls as slowly as a snowflake.
[wonder] It's the most beautiful thing you've ever seen. So you call your best friend.
…hello?
[softly] He picks up. And his voice is… gone. Just a deep rumble, like thunder far away.
This part is real. Sound is a vibration. Live ten times faster, and every voice reaches you ten times slower. Most of it drops so low that your ears can't hear it anymore.
[softly] You stand in the floating rain. And nobody in the world can hear you anymore.
Seven thirty. Your mom comes down to bake the birthday cake. [short pause] And she finds you.
She drops an egg. You have time to walk around the table… and catch it.
You say: "Mom, it's me." To her, it sounds like a bird chirping.
[sad] And for one second, she looks scared of you. For her, it's one second. For you, it's ten. The worst ten seconds of your life.
So you write on the whiteboard. To her, the words just appear. Then she writes back. It takes her half a minute. For you, it's five minutes. Five minutes of watching your mom's hand shake.
[softly] Not "what's happening". Not "what are you". [short pause] Are you hurt? [short pause] That's your mom.
Okay. Okay. Why did the snail…
Your dad calls an old friend from college. A physicist. Then, to calm everyone down, he starts telling a joke. [short pause] It takes ten of your minutes. It's about a snail.
The physicist brings a camera that films bullets. You write, she films, she plays it back slowly. That's how you talk now.
Then she starts writing. And her face changes.
Your days are getting shorter.
For everyone else, your day one lasted twenty-four hours. Day two, two and a half. Day three will be fifteen minutes. Every day you live is ten times shorter than the one before.
This part is real. It's one of the oldest puzzles in math. You can keep adding smaller and smaller pieces forever… and the total still stops at one number. It never gets past it.
And your number… is nine o'clock this morning. [long pause] Candles.
[whispers] You could live a thousand more days. And every single one of them fits before nine o'clock.

Then she writes one more line. Every time you sleep, you wake up faster, and nine o'clock runs away from you. But if you don't sleep… the clock keeps moving. Stay awake for nine more of your hours, and you'll be there.
[determined] You've been awake for seventeen hours. Nine more. You can do that.
Three hours later, your eyes are burning. You close them. [short pause] Just for a second.
[nervous] No. No no no. Day three. A hundred times. And you run to your mom.
This part is real. A quick step is about fifteen kilometers an hour. Times a hundred… that's faster than sound. You just broke the sound barrier. [short pause] By running to your mom.
[sad] Your shoes are smoking. Your parents have their hands over their ears. So you do the only safe thing. You leave.
[softly] You sit on the curb. Ten meters from the house you grew up in. And you've never felt so far away from it.
Day four. A thousand times. You wake up to headlights. The garbage truck. And running across the street in his dinosaur pajamas… your little brother. He heard the boom. He came looking for you.
Sixteen minutes. And you can't go fast.
So you push him like he's made of glass. Two minutes. Forty centimeters. Six minutes. One meter twenty.
Your arms shake. Every part of you wants to hurry. Your whole life, you were the slow one. [short pause] Now slow is the only thing that can save him.
[long pause] Twelve minutes. Two meters. The truck slides past, so close you could touch the mirror.
I know it's you.
[softly] Of course he does.
Then your mom comes to the window. She's writing on the glass. Backwards, so you can read it from outside.
Every letter takes her about a second. For you, that's seventeen minutes.
[softly] Seven hours later, it's finished. Come inside. We're not scared. [short pause] She's lying. You can see it in her hands. You go in anyway.
You walk at a millimeter per second now. [short pause] Snail. Turns out the bully was right. Just a little early.
Day five. Ten thousand times. Water won't pour anymore. Gravity is too slow for you.

And when you move your arm normally, your sleeve starts to smoke. It's the same reason meteors burn: they push through the air so fast that the air gets crazy hot. At ten thousand times, so does your hand.
Every day, you try. Stay awake. Day five, you make it nineteen hours. Day six, twenty-three. Day seven… twenty-five. So close you can smell the cake.
And this is real too. The record for staying awake is eleven days. A seventeen-year-old named Randy Gardner did it in 1964. [short pause] But he wasn't doing it in a world where nothing moves.
[softly] And then your family does something you'll never forget. If you can't come to the candles… they bring the candles to you.
For them, it takes a few seconds. For you, it takes a week.
Day seven. One million times faster. One second for them is twelve days for you. There's a tear on your mom's cheek. It hasn't moved in a week.
Grandma and Grandpa are in the doorway with a present. Grandpa is in the middle of a sentence. You're pretty sure it's the fishing story.
[softly] Your best friend is at the gate. Mid-sprint. One foot in the air. He's been in that same step for a week.
Race you, he always said. [short pause] You'd give anything to lose just one more time.
Day eight. Day nine. [short pause] Day ten. One billion times faster. One second for them… is thirty-two years for you.
And you see something no human has ever seen with their own eyes. [short pause] Light. Moving.

This part is real. Light travels three hundred thousand kilometers every second. At a billion times your speed, it crawls. About as fast as a turtle. Scientists have filmed this with a camera that takes a trillion pictures per second. You're seeing it live.
[softly] Everyone you love is in this kitchen. Mom, still holding the marker. Dad, halfway through laughing at his own joke. And your little brother, cheeks full of air, leaning toward nine candles.
Your whole life, you were late. For the bus. For school. For everything. [long pause] Today, you're early. So early that time itself can't catch up.
You've been awake for twenty hours. Seven more, and you'll be there when the candles go out. [short pause] But you're so tired. And every time you've closed your eyes… you woke up further away.
You put the last paper crane next to the cake. A thousand cranes. One wish.
[whispers] So… can you stay awake?
[warmly] Could YOU stay awake for seven more hours? Or would you close your eyes… and see what happens? Tell us in the comments. We read every single one.
Next time, we go the other way. What if every day… you got two times SMALLER?
Subscribe so you don't miss it. [short pause] And until then… be careful what you wish for.
